# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
# Review of the Varden County 30-hour week trial

This is a much stronger study than the Halden pilot. It is randomised and stratified, with a registered protocol, output from administrative records, and actual hours from timesheets. It also reports a negative result in the coverage-bound stratum honestly and labels the exploratory analysis as exploratory.

It confirms two of the concerns about the earlier paper:
- Measuring per-hour gains against scheduled hours inflates them (22% vs 12.5% here).
- Customer-facing work behaves differently from backlog work.

I checked the arithmetic and it is consistent:
- Hours: 37.9→33.0 is −12.9%; 37.6→31.2 is −17.0%.
- Output per actual hour: 0.979/0.871 gives +12.4–12.5%; 0.886/0.830 gives +6.7%.
- Scheduled-hours basis: 0.979/0.8 gives +22.4%.

The issues below are mostly about inference, cost, and interpretation.

## 1. The overtime is a cost the paper doesn't report

In case-processing offices, actual hours were 33.0 against 30 scheduled. That is about 3 hours a week of "overtime claimed", on top of full pay.

- **If the overtime is paid at a typical 1.5× premium**, it adds roughly 3 × 1.5 / 37.5 ≈ **12% to the salary bill**. Output per FTE also fell slightly, so labour cost per case closed could have risen by around **14%** in the stratum the paper presents as the success.
- **If it is time off in lieu**, the hours reduction is partly deferred rather than achieved.

The finding that output per employee was maintained is therefore partly bought back through overtime. The paper should report:
- whether overtime was paid or taken as leave, and at what rate;
- labour cost per unit of output, by arm and stratum.

For the county's question, "without loss of service", cost is the missing half of the answer.

## 2. The counter stratum's per-hour gain is probably utilisation, not productivity

Contact centres and service counters face exogenous demand. Under the control schedule, some staff time is idle, waiting for the next caller.

If fewer staff are present during the same opening hours, each one handles a larger share of the queue. Output per staff-hour rises because idle time falls, and the queue lengthens. The wait rising from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes is exactly what queueing theory predicts.

So "each hour worked was somewhat more productive" probably mislabels what happened. The +6.7% is most plausibly a shift of waiting from staff to the public, not faster or better work. This strengthens the paper's own argument about coverage-bound work, and the Discussion should say so.

A useful check would be handling time per contact, which the telephony system should record. If handling time was unchanged, the per-hour gain is utilisation.

## 3. Outcomes that are reported incompletely or not discussed

- **Waiting time and abandoned calls are given only as pre→post figures for treated offices.** Waiting time is a registered secondary outcome, so it should have a difference-in-differences estimate with a CI. The control trend is needed to rule out a county-wide change, such as a seasonal surge or a policy change that raised demand.
- **The repeat-contact rate worsened**, from 10.9% to 11.8%, a relative increase of about 8%. The text discusses quality only for case-processing and passes over this.
- **Repeat contacts may inflate the output measure.** If callers who abandoned or were unsatisfied call back, each return counts as another "contact handled". The true fall in service delivered may then be larger than −11.4%. Reporting unique contacts resolved would address this.
- **Table 1's quality row (3.1% v 3.0%)** doesn't say which figure is treated and which is control. It also isn't a DiD estimate and has no CI, unlike the rows above it.
- **Sick days and resignations have no CIs.** The paper should also say whether sickness is counted in days or hours. If the 30-hour week was worked as four days, some of the −29% is mechanical, because there are fewer scheduled days on which to be absent.

## 4. Inference with very few clusters

Standard errors are clustered by office, with 14 clusters in one stratum and **10 in the other**. Conventional cluster-robust standard errors are known to be too small with this few clusters, so CIs are too narrow and p-values too optimistic.

The counter-stratum output-per-hour interval (+0.4 to +13.3) only just excludes zero and is the most exposed. The paper should use one of:
- randomisation inference, which is natural here since assignment was randomised within strata;
- the wild cluster bootstrap;
- small-sample corrections, such as CR2 with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.

The other inferential points:
- **Report the registered primary analysis exactly as registered.** Was it pooled or by stratum? The Summary leads with the stratum contrast, but no pooled estimate is given. If the stratum-specific analysis was pre-specified, say so. Stratifying the randomisation does not by itself make subgroup effects a registered analysis.
- **Test the interaction formally.** The headline claim is that the effect differs by type of work, so it needs a test of the difference between −2.1% and −11.4%, not just two separate CIs.

## 5. Short-run measures in case-processing may flatter the result

- **Backlog.** Cases closed can be held up for a while by letting the queue grow, since work can be done "at any point within statutory deadlines". The limitations mention this, but backlog size and time-to-decision should be reported as outcomes now. The administrative systems will have them.
- **Case mix.** Staff under pressure may close quicker cases first. Reporting outcomes by case type, or weighted by complexity, would rule this out.
- **Appeal lag.** Appeals typically take months to be decided. Decisions from the later months of a nine-month trial won't have had time to be overturned, so the 3.1% v 3.0% comparison is incomplete. Consider following decisions up for a fixed period, or restricting to early-trial decisions.
- **Spillovers.** Check whether cases or calls can route between offices, through county-wide queues or overflow lines. If treated offices could pass work to control offices, the DiD is biased, and the bias would favour treatment for treated offices' metrics.
- **Control staff morale.** The paper mentions this, but the resignation contrast (3.9% vs 7.4%) makes it relevant. If control staff became demoralised, that would lower control output or raise control quits, and flatter treatment. Comparing the control arm's trends against their own pre-period, and against non-trial county offices if any exist, would help.

## 6. The meetings analysis may explain more than the authors suggest

The authors are appropriately cautious about the exploratory analysis. It can be pushed one step further, with the same caveats.

Suppose treated offices had the same 7.1 hours of meetings at baseline as control offices. This is untested, because meetings were measured only in month six. Then non-meeting work time compares as follows:

| | Actual hours | Meetings | Non-meeting hours |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control | 37.9 | 7.1 | 30.8 |
| Treated | 33.0 | 3.8 | 29.2 |

Non-meeting work time fell only about **5%**, while output fell 2.1%. Output per non-meeting hour therefore rose only about **3%**. On this rough accounting, most of the 12.5% per-hour gain is time removed from meetings, not faster casework.

That would support the authors' interpretation more strongly than "a substantial part" does. It also has a practical implication: much of the gain might be available without cutting hours at all.

Two caveats should be stated alongside it:
- The assumption of equal baseline meeting time is untested.
- With 7 offices, r = 0.71 has p ≈ 0.07 and a very wide CI.

For the 24-month confirmatory test, pre-period calendar data would make the analysis much stronger, if it can be recovered retrospectively.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Hours.** Report actual hours as a DiD with control, not only as treated pre→post. Control hours are described as "stable", but the figures aren't shown.
- **Scheduling.** Describe how the 30-hour rotas were organised in counter offices: four days, shorter days, or mixed. This affects both the sickness measure and coverage patterns.
- **Generalisability.** "Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work" is fair, and could note that statutory deadlines create unusual slack. Many private-sector backlogs carry costs of delay that these do not.
- **The Discussion's third conclusion** ("from 12.5% to 22%") is clear. It would read slightly better as "scheduled-hours measurement would have reported 22% rather than 12.5%".

## Overall

The design is credible, and the main qualitative conclusion is well supported: reduced hours affect backlog work and coverage-bound work very differently, and per-hour and per-employee productivity diverge. The improvements most likely to change interpretation are:

1. labour cost per unit of output, including overtime;
2. small-cluster-robust inference and a formal test of the stratum interaction;
3. DiD estimates for waiting time, abandoned calls, and quality, plus backlog and handling-time measures;
4. reframing the counter per-hour gain as a likely effect of higher utilisation, not productivity.
